mcqs.question: Three processes all arrive at time 0: P1 (burst 24), P2 (burst 3), P3 (burst 3), run in that order under FCFS. What is P3's waiting time?
options: 3, matching its own burst time
24, matching P1's burst time
0, since all processes arrived together
27, since P1 and P2 run for 24+3=27 units before P3 starts
mcqs.explanation: P3 must wait for both P1 (24) and P2 (3) to finish before it starts, so its waiting time is 24 + 3 = 27. Its own burst time, P1's burst time alone, and simultaneous arrival are each a different, incorrect number.

mcqs.question: Why is the convoy effect especially damaging when short I/O-bound jobs queue behind one long CPU-bound job?
options: The I/O-bound jobs can't even issue their quick I/O request until the long job finishes, idling the I/O device too
I/O-bound jobs cannot run under FCFS scheduling at all
The long job's I/O requests always fail while a convoy is forming
CPU-bound jobs are scheduled at a fundamentally different priority level under FCFS
mcqs.explanation: FCFS makes no distinction between job types — the short I/O-bound jobs simply can't get the CPU at all until the long job finishes, so the I/O device they'd otherwise be keeping busy sits idle too. FCFS has no separate priority levels, doesn't block I/O-bound jobs categorically, and doesn't cause I/O failures.

mcqs.question: Using the same three processes (P1=24, P2=3, P3=3, all arrive at 0) but scheduled with SJF instead of FCFS, what is the new average waiting time?
options: 17, identical to FCFS since total work is unchanged
0, since SJF eliminates all waiting
30, the sum of all burst times
mcqs.explanation: Running P2 and P3 first (0 and 3 waiting respectively) then P1 (6 waiting) gives (0+3+6)/3 = 3 — dramatically better than FCFS's 17 despite identical total work, because reordering shifts who waits, not how much total work exists. It isn't 0 (P1 and P3 still wait something) and 30 is simply the sum of bursts, not an average wait.

mcqs.question: Since an OS can't know a process's future burst time in advance, how do real schedulers approximate SJF's ranking?
options: They ask the user to manually specify each process's expected runtime
They predict future burst length using exponential averaging of that process's past burst behavior
They assume every process has an identical burst time
They run every process for a fixed trial period and then guess randomly
mcqs.explanation: Exponential averaging of past bursts (next = α × actual_previous + (1-α) × previous_prediction) is the standard technique, using a process's own history as a proxy for its next burst. Users aren't consulted for this, processes aren't assumed identical, and there's no random guessing after a fixed trial.

mcqs.question: P1 (arrival 0, burst 8) is running when P2 (arrival 1, burst 4) shows up. Under SRTF, what happens at time 1?
options: P1 keeps running uninterrupted since it started first
Both processes run simultaneously on the same core
P2 waits for P1 to fully complete since SRTF only preempts at arrival time zero
P1 is preempted immediately because P2's burst (4) is shorter than P1's remaining time (7)
mcqs.explanation: SRTF compares the new arrival's burst against the running process's *remaining* time at every arrival; here 4 < 7, so P1 is preempted right away. SRTF doesn't protect a process just for starting first, doesn't run two processes on one core simultaneously, and preempts at any arrival, not only at time zero.

mcqs.question: Why isn't "SJF minimizes average waiting time, so it's simply the best scheduler" a complete conclusion?
options: Because SJF's optimality is mathematically incorrect
Because SJF can starve long jobs indefinitely if shorter jobs keep arriving, which the average alone doesn't reveal
Because SJF only works with exactly two processes
Because SJF's optimality claim only applies to non-CPU-bound workloads
mcqs.explanation: SJF's optimality is real but only about the average; a continuous stream of short arrivals can starve a long job forever, a worst-case failure the average metric hides completely. The proof itself is correct, it works for any number of processes, and the optimality claim isn't restricted to a particular workload type.
